analysis.one_liner: Gave Medicare doctors a temporary payment raise and let companies stretch out underfunded pension contributions.
analysis.headline: The House passed a sweeping health care overhaul under this bill number 220-215, but the Senate never voted on that text; it instead passed a narrow Medicare doctor-payment and pension-relief bill under the same number, which became law with a 417-1 House concurrence vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill number had two lives. Introduced in October 2009, it was the Affordable Health Care for America Act: a health insurance marketplace with a government-run public option, a requirement that almost everyone carry coverage, an 8% payroll charge on employers who do not offer insurance, new insurer rules, and a 5.4% income surtax on individuals making over $500,000 to help pay for it. The House passed it 220-215 on November 7, 2009. The Senate put it on its calendar and never debated that version. Instead, in June 2010 the Senate passed, under the same bill number, a completely different and much narrower law: a 2.2% Medicare physician payment update for June through November 2010 (averting the deep formula-driven cut otherwise scheduled), a tighter hospital billing rule, an IRS data match to screen Medicare providers with delinquent tax debts, and relief letting companies with underfunded pensions spread their required contributions over more years. The House agreed to the Senate version 417-1 and the President signed it as Public Law 111-192.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors on Medicare, because doctors were spared a large payment cut that threatened access to care; physicians, who kept higher Medicare reimbursement; and companies (and union plans) sponsoring underfunded defined-benefit pensions, which won years of extra time to make up funding shortfalls from the 2008 market crash.

how_it_helps.text: Sets the Medicare physician payment update at 2.2% for June 1 through November 30, 2010, in place of the cut the payment formula would otherwise have produced.

Lets sponsors of single-employer defined-benefit pension plans elect 9-year or 15-year amortization of funding shortfalls (instead of the usual 7 years) for plan years 2008-2011, and adds installments back for firms paying executives over $1 million or declaring extraordinary dividends and stock redemptions.

Lets multiemployer (largely union) pension plans spread net investment losses from the two years after August 2008 over as long as 30 years and smooth asset values over up to 10 years, with notice to participants and the pension insurer.
Authorizes Treasury to share delinquent tax debt information with HHS so Medicare can deny enrollment or apply enhanced oversight to providers who owe taxes.

As originally introduced and passed by the House, the same bill number created a health insurance exchange with a public option, barred preexisting-condition exclusions and lifetime limits, required dependent coverage up to age 27, and imposed a 5.4% surtax on incomes over $500,000 to finance coverage expansions.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and the Medicare program bear the cost of the physician payment increase; hospitals give up billing latitude under the tightened three-day payment window rule, which bars administrative or judicial review; and the federal pension insurance backstop takes on added long-term risk because companies paying pension contributions more slowly could fail later with larger unfunded promises.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, hospitals, and the pension insurer

drawbacks.text: Pension relief lets companies pay required pension contributions more slowly — stretching single-employer shortfall repayments up to 15 years and multiemployer investment losses up to 30 years — deferring risk to the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation and to workers if a sponsor later fails with a bigger unfunded hole.

The bill itself imposes penalty installments on firms that pay executives over $1 million or declare extraordinary dividends and stock redemptions while using the relief — an acknowledgment that otherwise the funding deferral could bankroll payouts to shareholders and executives.

The physician update is explicitly temporary (June 1 through November 30, 2010) and the law says later years must be computed as if it had never applied, leaving the underlying payment formula's future cuts untouched.

The tightened hospital three-day payment window bundles pre-admission services into the inpatient payment and prohibits any administrative or judicial review of that determination, and bars Medicare from reopening previously bundled claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: What became law was a reasonable, narrow stopgap: seniors were spared a doctor-access crisis, and pension plans battered by the 2008 crash got breathing room rather than immediate contribution spikes that could push sponsors into benefit freezes or termination. The real costs are deferred rather than eliminated — the pension insurer absorbs extra downside risk, Medicare's underlying payment formula problem was only papered over for six months, and hospitals absorbed a billing rule with no appeal. The larger story is procedural: the consequential health overhaul originally carried under this number was never given a Senate vote here.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate never voted on the sweeping health overhaul the House passed under this number; it instead passed a completely different, narrow Medicare-doctor-payment and pension-relief bill under the same bill number by unanimous consent, and the House accepted that swap 417-1.

narrative.text: Introduced October 29, 2009 as the Affordable Health Care for America Act, creating a health insurance exchange with a public option, near-universal coverage requirements, new insurer rules, and a 5.4% surtax on high incomes to pay for it.
The House passed that version 220-215 on November 7, 2009, with Democrats voting 219-39 in favor and Republicans 1-176 against after adopting the Stupak abortion-funding restriction.
The Senate received the bill in November 2009 and placed it on its legislative calendar under General Orders, but never brought the House health reform text to a debate or vote.

On June 18, 2010 the Senate passed, by unanimous consent under this same bill number, a different measure retitled the Preservation of Access to Care for Medicare Beneficiaries and Pension Relief Act of 2010: a 2.2% physician payment update, the hospital three-day payment window change, an IRS-HHS fraud screen, and pension funding relief.
The House agreed to the Senate amendments 417-1 on June 24, 2010 — 247-1 among Democrats and 170-0 among Republicans — and the President signed it into law as Public Law 111-192 on June 25.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physicians kept Medicare pay at a raised rate instead of a formula cut, and companies and union plans with underfunded pensions won years of deferral on required contributions. The Senate also kept complete control of the health reform process by never voting on the House text under this number. Who Came Out Ahead Short: "Doctors and underfunded-pension sponsors"

sides.party_line_note: House passage of the original health reform split sharply by party — 219-39 among Democrats versus 1-176 among Republicans — but the final law drew almost no opposition: the Senate passed it by unanimous consent and the House concurred 417-1 (247-1 Democrats, 170-0 Republicans).

industries.note: The 2.2% Medicare update replaced a large formula-driven payment cut for the second half of 2010; doctors kept higher Medicare pay, and seniors avoided doctors' offices closing to Medicare patients. The benefit to the industry ran alongside patients' access to care.

Single-employer and multiemployer plans won years of extra time to make up funding shortfalls caused by the 2008 crash, easing pressure on employers and avoiding immediate benefit cuts to workers. But paying contributions more slowly shifts long-term risk to the federal pension insurer if a sponsor later fails; anti-abuse rules claw back installments from firms paying executives over $1 million or doing extraordinary dividends and buybacks.

The tightened three-day payment window forces hospitals to bundle more pre-admission services into the inpatient payment, bars them from reopening previously bundled claims, and prohibits any administrative or judicial review of the determination. Hospital revenue interest ran against the provision's Medicare savings.
The pension insurer gets notice of relief elections and limits on benefit increases, but deferring sponsor contributions raises the size of the hole it could inherit if plans terminate later.
